abstract: <jats:p>Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC) plays pivotal roles in the carbon fixation of photosynthesis and a variety of metabolic and stress pathways. <jats:italic>Suaeda aralocaspica</jats:italic> belongs to a single-cellular C<jats:sub>4</jats:sub> species and carries out a photosynthetic pathway in an unusually elongated chlorenchyma cell, which is expected to have PEPCs with different characteristics. To identify the different isoforms of <jats:italic>PEPC</jats:italic> genes in <jats:italic>S. aralocaspica</jats:italic> and comparatively analyze their expression and regulation patterns as well as the biochemical and enzymatic properties in this study, we characterized a bacterial-type PEPC (BTPC; SaPEPC-4) in addition to the two plant-type PEPCs (PTPCs; SaPEPC-1 and SaPEPC-2) using a genome-wide identification. <jats:italic>SaPEPC-4</jats:italic> presented a lower expression level in all test combinations with an unknown function; two SaPTPCs showed distinct subcellular localizations and different spatiotemporal expression patterns but positively responded to abiotic stresses. Compared to <jats:italic>SaPEPC-2</jats:italic>, the expression of <jats:italic>SaPEPC-1</jats:italic> specifically in chlorenchyma cell tissues was much more active with the progression of development and under various stresses, particularly sensitive to light, implying the involvement of <jats:italic>SaPEPC-1</jats:italic> in a C<jats:sub>4</jats:sub> photosynthetic pathway. In contrast, <jats:italic>SaPEPC-2</jats:italic> was more like a non-photosynthetic PEPC. The expression trends of two SaPTPCs in response to light, development, and abiotic stresses were also matched with the changes in PEPC activity <jats:italic>in vivo</jats:italic> (native) or <jats:italic>in vitro</jats:italic> (recombinant), and the biochemical properties of the two recombinant SaPTPCs were similar in response to various effectors while the catalytic efficiency, substrate affinity, and enzyme activity of SaPEPC-2 were higher than that of SaPEPC-1 <jats:italic>in vitro.</jats:italic> All the different properties between these two SaPTPCs might be involved in transcriptional (e.g., specific <jats:italic>cis</jats:italic>-elements), posttranscriptional [e.g., 5′-untranslated region (5′-UTR) secondary structure], or translational (e.g., PEPC phosphorylation/dephosphorylation) regulatory events. The comparative studies on the different isoforms of the PEPC gene family in <jats:italic>S. aralocaspica</jats:italic> may help to decipher their exact role in C<jats:sub>4</jats:sub> photosynthesis, plant growth/development, and stress resistance.</jats:p>
title: Genome-Wide Identification and Analysis of the Phosphoenolpyruvate Carboxylase Gene Family in Suaeda aralocaspica, an Annual Halophyte With Single-Cellular C4 Anatomy

abstract: <jats:p>A Gram-negative, non-spore-forming, endophytic bacterium, strain YC6886<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>, was isolated from the root of a halophyte,<jats:italic>Rosa rugosa</jats:italic>, which inhabits coastal areas of Namhae Island off the southern coast of Korea. Cells were non-motile, obligately aerobic rods and formed pale-yellow colonies. The isolate grew at 4–32 °C (optimum 25–28 °C) and at pH 6.5–9.5 (optimum pH 7.5) and grew optimally with 2–3 % (w/v) NaCl, but NaCl was not an absolute requirement for growth. Strain YC6886<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>produced yellow carotenoid pigments. Strain YC6886<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>exhibited the highest 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity with<jats:italic>Haloferula sargassicola</jats:italic>MN1-1037<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>(97.4 %). Sequence similarities between strain YC6886<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>and other members of the genus<jats:italic>Haloferula</jats:italic>were 93.9–94.7 %. DNA–DNA relatedness between strain YC6886<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>and<jats:italic>H. sargassicola</jats:italic>KCTC 22202<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>and<jats:italic>Haloferula rosea</jats:italic>KCTC 22201<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>was 27 and 15 %, respectively. The major fatty acids were iso-C<jats:sub>14 : 0</jats:sub>, C<jats:sub>16 : 0</jats:sub>and C<jats:sub>16 : 1</jats:sub>ω9<jats:italic>c</jats:italic>and minor components were C<jats:sub>14 : 0</jats:sub>, C<jats:sub>18 : 0</jats:sub>and anteiso-C<jats:sub>15 : 0</jats:sub>. The major respiratory quinone was menaquinone 9 and the DNA G+C content was 58.5 mol%. The polar lipid profile was composed of diphosphatidylglycerol, phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylglycerol, an unknown phospholipid and an unknown phosphoglycolipid. On the basis of phenotypic, chemotaxonomic, DNA–DNA hybridization and phylogenetic analysis, strain YC6886<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>represents a novel species in the genus<jats:italic>Haloferula</jats:italic>, for which the name<jats:italic>Haloferula luteola</jats:italic>sp. nov. is proposed. The type strain is YC6886<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>( = KCTC 22447<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> = DSM 21608<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>). An emended description of the genus<jats:italic>Haloferula</jats:italic>is also presented.</jats:p>
title: Haloferula luteola sp. nov., an endophytic bacterium isolated from the root of a halophyte, Rosa rugosa, and emended description of the genus Haloferula

abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>A full accounting of net greenhouse gas balance (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NGHGB</jats:styled-content>) and greenhouse gas intensity (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">GHGI</jats:styled-content>) was examined in an annual coastal reclaimed saline Jerusalem artichoke‐fallow cropping system under various soil practices including soil tillage, soil ameliorant, and crop residue amendments. Seasonal fluxes of soil carbon dioxide (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CO</jats:styled-content><jats:sub>2</jats:sub>), methane (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CH</jats:styled-content><jats:sub>4</jats:sub>), and nitrous oxide (N<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>O) were measured using static chamber method, and the net ecosystem exchange of <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CO</jats:styled-content><jats:sub>2</jats:sub> (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NEE</jats:styled-content>) was determined by the difference between soil heterotrophic respiration (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case"><jats:italic>R</jats:italic><jats:sub>H</jats:sub></jats:styled-content>) and net primary production (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NPP</jats:styled-content>). Relative to no‐tillage, rotary tillage significantly decreased the <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NPP</jats:styled-content> of Jerusalem artichoke while it had no significant effects on the annual <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case"><jats:italic>R</jats:italic><jats:sub>H</jats:sub></jats:styled-content>. Rotary tillage increased <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CH</jats:styled-content><jats:sub>4</jats:sub> emissions, while seasonal or annual soil N<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>O emissions did not statistically differ between the two tillage treatments. Compared with the control plots, soil ameliorant or straw amendment enhanced <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case"><jats:italic>R</jats:italic><jats:sub>H</jats:sub></jats:styled-content>, soil <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CH</jats:styled-content><jats:sub>4,</jats:sub> and N<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>O emissions under the both tillage regimes. Annual <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NGHGB</jats:styled-content> was negative for all the field treatments, as a consequence of net ecosystem <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CO</jats:styled-content><jats:sub>2</jats:sub> sequestration exceeding the <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CO</jats:styled-content><jats:sub>2</jats:sub>‐equivalents released as <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CH</jats:styled-content><jats:sub>4</jats:sub> and N<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>O emissions, which indicates that Jerusalem artichoke‐fallow cropping system served as a net sink of <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">GHG</jats:styled-content>s. The annual net <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NGHGB</jats:styled-content> and <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">GHGI</jats:styled-content> were estimated to be 11–21% and 4–8% lower in the <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NT</jats:styled-content> than in <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RT</jats:styled-content> cropping systems, respectively. Soil ameliorant and straw amendments greatly increased <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NPP</jats:styled-content> and thus significantly decreased the negative annual net <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NGHGB</jats:styled-content>. Overall, higher <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NPP</jats:styled-content> but lower climatic impacts of coastal saline bioenergy production would be simultaneously achieved by Jerusalem artichoke cultivation under no‐tillage with improved saline soil conditions in southeast China.</jats:p>
title: Annual net greenhouse gas balance in a halophyte (Helianthus tuberosus) bioenergy cropping system under various soil practices in Southeast China

abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Halophyte <jats:italic>Halogeton glomeratus</jats:italic> mostly grows in saline desert areas in arid and semi‐arid regions and is able to adapt to adverse conditions such as salinity and drought. Earlier transcriptomic studies revealed activation of the <jats:italic>HgS2</jats:italic> gene in the leaf of <jats:italic>H. glomeratus</jats:italic> seedlings when exposed to saline conditions. To identify the properties of <jats:italic>HgS2</jats:italic> in <jats:italic>H. glomeratus</jats:italic>, we used yeast transformation and overexpression in <jats:italic>Arabidopsis</jats:italic>. Yeast cells genetically transformed with <jats:italic>HgS2</jats:italic> exhibited K<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> uptake and Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> efflux compared with control (empty vector). Stable overexpression of <jats:italic>HgS2</jats:italic> in Arabidopsis improved its resistance to salt stress and led to a notable rise in seed germination in salinity conditions compared to the wild type (WT). Transgenic <jats:italic>Arabidopsis</jats:italic> regulated ion homeostasis in plant cells by increasing Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> absorption and decreasing K<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> efflux in leaves, while reducing Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> absorption and K<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> efflux in roots. In addition, overexpression of <jats:italic>HgS2</jats:italic> altered transcription levels of stress response genes and regulated different metabolic pathways in roots and leaves of <jats:italic>Arabidopsis</jats:italic>. These results offer new insights into the role of <jats:italic>HgS2</jats:italic> in plants' salt tolerance.</jats:p>
title: HgS2, a novel salt‐responsive gene from the Halophyte Halogeton glomeratus, confers salt tolerance in transgenic Arabidopsis

abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p><jats:italic>Myo</jats:italic>‐inositol and its metabolic derivatives such as pinitol, galactinol, and raffinose affect growth and development and are also involved in stress adaptation. Previous studies have identified <jats:italic>myo</jats:italic>‐inositol transporters (INTs) as transporters of Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> from root to shoot in the halophyte ice plant (<jats:italic>Mesembryanthemum crystallinum</jats:italic>). We found that the supply of <jats:italic>myo</jats:italic>‐inositol could alleviate the dehydration effects of salt‐stressed ice plant seedlings by decreasing the Na/K ratio in roots and increasing the Na/K ratio in shoots. Analyses of the uptake of exogenous <jats:italic>myo</jats:italic>‐inositol revealed that ice plant seedlings contained intrinsic high‐affinity transporters and inducible low‐affinity uptake systems. The presence of Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> facilitated both high‐ and low‐affinity <jats:italic>myo</jats:italic>‐inositol uptake. Six <jats:italic>INT</jats:italic> genes were identified from the ice plant transcriptome and named <jats:italic>McINT1a</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>1b</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>2</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>4a</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>4b</jats:italic>, and <jats:italic>4c</jats:italic>, according to the classification of the Arabidopsis <jats:italic>INT</jats:italic> family. In seedlings treated with <jats:italic>myo</jats:italic>‐inositol, salt, or <jats:italic>myo</jats:italic>‐inositol plus salt, the expression patterns of all <jats:italic>McINT</jats:italic> members differed in shoot and root, which indicates organ‐specific regulation of <jats:italic>McINTs</jats:italic> by salt and <jats:italic>myo</jats:italic>‐inositol. The expression of <jats:italic>McINT2</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>4a</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>4b</jats:italic>, and <jats:italic>4c</jats:italic> was induced by salt stress in shoot and root, but that of <jats:italic>McINT1a</jats:italic> and <jats:italic>1b</jats:italic> was salt‐induced only in shoot. The expression of pinitol biosynthesis gene <jats:italic>IMT1</jats:italic> was induced by salt and <jats:italic>myo</jats:italic>‐inositol, and their combination had a synergistic effect on the accumulation of pinitol. Supply of <jats:italic>myo</jats:italic>‐inositol to salt‐treated seedlings alleviated the detrimental effects by maintaining a low root Na/K ratio and providing precursors for the synthesis of compatible solute to maintain the osmotic balance.</jats:p>
title: Myo‐inositol transport and metabolism participate in salt tolerance of halophyte ice plant seedlings

abstract: <jats:sec><jats:title>Introduction</jats:title><jats:p>New alternate food and pharma sources, halophyte plants have long been displaying exceptional nutritional and functional qualities.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Methods</jats:title><jats:p>Present investigations were carried out to explore three important halophyte herbs; <jats:italic>Anabasis articulata</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>Lycium shawii</jats:italic>, and <jats:italic>Zilla spinosa</jats:italic>,harvested from deserts, for phytochemical composition and potential food application.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title><jats:p>Plant leaves, converted into powders showed significant amounts of ash, fiber, and important minerals as contents (%) of ash and fiber in <jats:italic>Anabasis articulata</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>Lycium shawii</jats:italic>, and <jats:italic>Zilla spinosa</jats:italic> were 6.39 and 6.79, 8.19 and 9.14, and 4.35 and 8.87, respectively, while Mg, Zn, Cu and Mn were significantly higher in <jats:italic>Anabasis articulata</jats:italic>, with values 52.40, 50.59, 16.33 and 48.25 mg/kg, respectively, whereas <jats:italic>Zilla spinosa</jats:italic> presented Fe as 120.95 mg/kg, highest from all. Total phenolic contents (45.92 mg gallic acid equivalent/g), total flavonoid contents (11.31 mg quercetin equivalent/g) and total antioxidant activity (22.85 mg Trolox/g) were found highest in ethanolic extract of <jats:italic>Lycium shawii</jats:italic>, while in remaining two plants these values were also prominent. Extracts of these three halophytes leaves exhibited prominent antimicrobial activities, as calculated zone of inhibitions (mm) were comparable to reference drugs. Incorporation of powders of all three halophytes resulted in significant increment in ash fiber and minerals (Mg, Zn, Fe, Cu and Mn) content of biscuits but with slight decrement in moisture, fat and protein. Formulated biscuits were also found boosted in total phenolic and flavonoid contents with elevated antioxidant activity as a result of incorporation of halophytes powders. Assessment of biscuits revealed that 5% levels of all halophyte’s powders produced acceptable product in terms of color, taste, texture and overall acceptability. Thus, halophyte plant powders and extracts could be used as new and sustainable source for food and pharma products.</jats:p></jats:sec>
